newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Insurance openness in China a long way off -analyst.
newsitem.headline: Insurance openness in China a long way off -analyst.

text.p: An open Chinese insurance market is still a long way off despite central bank assurances that liberalisation measures will be expanded, a Chinese insurance law adviser said on Friday.

"Insurance is still a delicate subject in China and its liberalisation is likely to be much slower than other financial sectors like banking," Su Min, Chinese law adviser with Sook Lin & Bok in Singapore, told Reuters.
"Any licences issued will take some considerable time to arrive," Su said.
Hopes of more than 70 insurers with licence applications pending were raised last week after comments from Dai Xianglong, governor of the People's Bank of China.
"China will continue to expand the opening of its finance industry to foreigners," Dai told China Securities newspaper.

The China insurance market is considered the jewel in the Asian crown by Western insurers and is an area in which international trade officials want to see some definite movement before admitting China to the World Trade Organisation.
Analysts at Sigma, the research arm of Swiss Reinsurance Co RUKZ.Z, peg real growth at 16.5 percent and 25 percent for non-life and life insurance branches respectively up to 2000.
Insurance industry sources say China generated premium income of about US$8 billion in 1996 and consider this to be just a fraction of what the market could eventually be worth.
The World Bank predicts premium volume will hit US$30 billion by 2000.
The bulk of premiums is still controlled by former state monopoly, the People's Insurance Company of China (PICC) and breaking its grip will be tough, Su said.
"We saw a limited step last year," said Su, referring to the establishment in 1996 of four domestic insurers by the Chinese authorities to rival PICC.
"But insurance is still too immature as a sector to let a lot of foreigners in," he said.
"Also the officials steering the policy changes are former PICC officials and they are not going to want to let too many in," Su added.
Some long-standing applicants have similar perspectives.
"I'll believe it (more foreign licences) when I see it," said the Asia regional manager of one European insurance group who declined to be identified.
"I suppose it was always unlikely that a British company would get a licence before the Hong Kong handover," said the manager of one UK insurer with a representative office in China.
